Inside a long current-carrying solenoid the magnetic field is directed along its axis, here the X-axis. The protons also move along the X-axis, so their velocity is parallel to \(\vec{B}\).

The magnetic force is \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\), and \(\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = 0\) when the two vectors are parallel. No force acts, so the beam keeps moving in a straight line.

answers.label: C
answers.working:
A particle of charge \(q\) and mass \(m\) accelerated from rest through a potential difference \(V\) gains kinetic energy \(qV\), so its momentum is \(p = \sqrt{2mqV}\) and its de Broglie wavelength is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\).

For the same \(V\), the particle with the smallest product \(mq\) has the largest wavelength. The electron has the same magnitude of charge as the proton but about 1836 times less mass, while the deuteron and alpha particle are heavier still (the alpha also has double charge). So the electron has the smallest \(mq\).

So the answer is option (c), the electron.

answers.label: B
answers.working:
The susceptibility of a diamagnetic material is negative and practically independent of temperature.

For a paramagnetic material the susceptibility follows Curie's law, \(\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}\): it decreases as the temperature rises, because thermal agitation disturbs the alignment of the atomic magnetic dipoles.

So the answer is option (b), paramagnetic.
answers.flag: A ferromagnet's susceptibility also falls as temperature rises (and it turns paramagnetic above the Curie temperature), so (c) is arguably also true as printed; (b) is the textbook answer via Curie's law. The paper also writes susceptibility as \psi instead of the usual \chi.

In forward bias the p-side is connected to the positive terminal. The applied voltage opposes the barrier potential, so the depletion region becomes narrower and majority carriers cross the junction easily.

The diode then offers a low resistance and a large current (of the order of mA) flows. Options (a) and (c) describe reverse bias, and in forward bias the depletion region narrows, not widens, so (d) is wrong.

So the answer is option (b).

Consider an electric dipole of charges \(-q\) at A and \(+q\) at B, separated by \(2l\), so its dipole moment is \(p = q(2l)\), directed from \(-q\) to \(+q\). Let O be the centre of the dipole and P a point on its axis at distance \(r\) from O, on the side of \(+q\).

Then \(BP = r - l\) and \(AP = r + l\).

**Field due to \(+q\)** at P, directed away from B along the axis (along \(\vec{p}\)):

\(E_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\,\dfrac{q}{(r - l)^2}\).

**Field due to \(-q\)** at P, directed towards A (opposite to \(\vec{p}\)):

\(E_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\,\dfrac{q}{(r + l)^2}\).

Since \(r - l < r + l\), \(E_1 > E_2\), and the resultant field is along \(\vec{p}\):

\(E = E_1 - E_2 = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{1}{(r - l)^2} - \dfrac{1}{(r + l)^2}\right] = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\,\dfrac{(r + l)^2 - (r - l)^2}{(r^2 - l^2)^2}\).

Now \((r + l)^2 - (r - l)^2 = 4rl\), so

\(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\,\dfrac{4qlr}{(r^2 - l^2)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\,\dfrac{2(q \cdot 2l)r}{(r^2 - l^2)^2}\).

Using \(p = q \cdot 2l\):

\(E = \left(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\right)\dfrac{2pr}{(r^2 - l^2)^2}\), directed along the dipole moment. Hence proved.

(For a short dipole, \(l \ll r\), this reduces to \(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\,\dfrac{2p}{r^3}\).)

answers.value: \(40\ \Omega\) connected in parallel with the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor
answers.working:
Both branches (3 \(\Omega\), M, 6 \(\Omega\)) and (4 \(\Omega\), N, 10 \(\Omega\)) are connected across the same two points, the left junction and O, so the same voltage is applied across each. M and N will be at the same potential when the potential drops across 3 \(\Omega\) and 4 \(\Omega\) are equal, that is when the bridge is balanced:

\(\dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{4}{X} \Rightarrow X = 8\ \Omega\).

So the 10 \(\Omega\) arm must be reduced to 8 \(\Omega\). A resistance added in series would increase it, so the resistance \(R\) must be connected **in parallel** with the 10 \(\Omega\) resistor:

\(\dfrac{10R}{10 + R} = 8 \Rightarrow 10R = 80 + 8R \Rightarrow R = 40\ \Omega\).

**Check:** upper branch current \(= \dfrac{2}{3 + 6} = \dfrac{2}{9}\ \mathrm{A}\), drop across 3 \(\Omega\) \(= \dfrac{2}{3}\ \mathrm{V}\). Lower branch current \(= \dfrac{2}{4 + 8} = \dfrac{1}{6}\ \mathrm{A}\), drop across 4 \(\Omega\) \(= \dfrac{2}{3}\ \mathrm{V}\). The drops are equal, so M and N are at the same potential.

So a \(40\ \Omega\) resistor should be connected in parallel with the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor.

**Upper branch:** the 2 V (1 \(\Omega\)) and 4 V (3 \(\Omega\)) cells are in series and drawn the same way round, so they aid each other:

\(E_1 = 2 + 4 = 6\ \mathrm{V}\), \(r_1 = 1 + 3 = 4\ \Omega\).

**Lower branch:** \(E_2 = 6\ \mathrm{V}\), \(r_2 = 12\ \Omega\).

The two branches are in parallel with like terminals together.

**(a)** For cells in parallel,

\(E = \dfrac{\dfrac{E_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{E_2}{r_2}}{\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{6}{4} + \dfrac{6}{12}}{\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{12}} = \dfrac{2}{1/3} = 6\ \mathrm{V}\).

(This is expected: both branches have the same emf of 6 V, so no current circulates between them on open circuit.)

**(b)** \(\dfrac{1}{r} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{4}{12} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(r = 3\ \Omega\).

The battery has emf 6 V and internal resistance \(3\ \Omega\).

Consider a circular coil of radius \(R\) with \(n\) turns carrying current \(I\), with centre O. Take a small current element \(I\,d\vec{l}\) on the coil.

By the Biot-Savart law, the field at O due to this element is

\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,dl\,\sin\theta}{R^2}\),

where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(d\vec{l}\) and the radius vector to O. Every element of the coil is tangential, so \(d\vec{l}\) is perpendicular to the radius: \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\sin\theta = 1\).

Also, by the right-hand rule, the field due to every element at O points in the same direction, perpendicular to the plane of the coil. So the contributions simply add:

\(B_{\text{one turn}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}\oint dl = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\).

For \(n\) turns the fields add, so

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2R}\),

directed along the axis of the coil, perpendicular to its plane (given by the right-hand thumb rule).

answers.value: (i) Diffraction at a single slit; (ii) a central white band with a few coloured bands on either side; (iii) light behaves as a wave
answers.working:
Kabir's pattern has bright bands of equal width, equally spaced: this is **interference** (as in Young's double slit experiment). Neha's pattern has a wide central bright band with narrower and fainter bands on both sides.

**(i)** Neha observed **diffraction of light at a single slit**.

**(ii)** With white light, Kabir would see a **white central bright band** (all colours have zero path difference there and reinforce). On either side there would be a few **coloured bands**, each with violet/blue nearer the centre and red farther out, because the fringe width \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\) is smaller for shorter wavelengths. Farther from the centre the colours overlap and the screen looks almost uniformly white, so only a few fringes are visible.

**(iii)** Interference and diffraction can be explained only if light is a **wave**. So both concluded that light has a wave nature.

**Diagram (described):** a plane reflecting surface XY. A plane wavefront AB is incident obliquely on it, with A just touching the surface. Incident rays (perpendicular to AB) reach the surface at A and, from B, at C. The normals at A and C are drawn, the angle of incidence \(i\) is marked between the incident ray and the normal, and the reflected wavefront CD is drawn with the reflected rays and the angle of reflection \(r\).

**Proof:** Let \(v\) be the speed of light in the medium. When point A of the wavefront touches the surface, point B still has to travel BC to reach the surface at C. Let this take time \(t\), so \(BC = vt\).

According to Huygens' principle, A becomes a source of secondary wavelets. In time \(t\), the wavelet from A spreads into a hemisphere of radius \(AD = vt\) in the same medium. The tangent drawn from C to this hemisphere touches it at D, and CD is the reflected wavefront.

Now compare triangles ABC and CDA:

- \(\angle ABC = \angle CDA = 90^\circ\) (a ray is perpendicular to its wavefront),
- \(BC = AD = vt\),
- AC is common.

So the two triangles are congruent (RHS), and therefore \(\angle BAC = \angle DCA\).

The angle between the incident wavefront AB and the surface equals the angle of incidence: \(\angle BAC = i\). The angle between the reflected wavefront CD and the surface equals the angle of reflection: \(\angle DCA = r\).

Hence \(i = r\): the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. Also the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in the same plane.

answers.working:
**(a)** Comparing \(e = 495\sin(100\pi t)\) with \(e = E_0\sin\omega t\): \(E_0 = 495\ \mathrm{V}\).

\(E_{rms} = \dfrac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{495}{1{\cdot}414} \approx 350\ \mathrm{V}\).

\(I_{rms} = \dfrac{E_{rms}}{R} = \dfrac{350}{70} = 5\ \mathrm{A}\).

**(b)** For a solenoid with an iron core, \(L = \dfrac{\mu_0\mu_r N^2 A}{l}\), with \(N = 25\), \(l = 0{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{m}\), \(A = 1 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}\) and \(\mu_r = 3000\) (iron, from the table).

\(L = \dfrac{4 \times 3{\cdot}14 \times 10^{-7} \times 3000 \times 25^2 \times 1 \times 10^{-4}}{0{\cdot}2}\)

\(L = \dfrac{4 \times 3{\cdot}14 \times 10^{-7} \times 3000 \times 625 \times 10^{-4}}{0{\cdot}2} \approx 1{\cdot}18 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{H}\) (about \(1{\cdot}18\ \mathrm{mH}\)).

**(c)** Soft iron is preferred because it has a **high permeability** (so the flux is concentrated and linked well between the coils) and a **narrow hysteresis loop** (low retentivity and coercivity), so the energy lost as heat in each cycle of magnetisation (hysteresis loss) is much smaller than in steel.

answers.value: (i) BE/A curve rising to a peak of about \(8{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{MeV}\) at Fe-56 (most stable); (ii) \(L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\); (iii) \(\lambda \approx 364{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{nm}\)
answers.working:
**(i)** The graph has mass number \(A\) on the x-axis (0 to about 240) and binding energy per nucleon (in MeV) on the y-axis (0 to about 9 MeV). Its main features:

- For light nuclei the curve rises steeply from about \(1{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{MeV}\) (\(^2\mathrm{H}\)), with small peaks for \(^4\mathrm{He}\), \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\) and \(^{16}\mathrm{O}\).
- It reaches a broad maximum of about \(8{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{MeV}\) near \(A = 56\). This point is marked \(^{56}\mathrm{Fe}\) (iron), the **most stable nucleus**.
- For heavier nuclei it falls slowly, to about \(7{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{MeV}\) for \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\).

**(ii)** It means the angular momentum of an electron in a Bohr orbit cannot have just any value: it can only be an integral multiple of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\),

\(L = mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), where \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

So the electron can revolve only in those orbits for which this condition holds (the stationary orbits).

**(iii)** For the Balmer series, \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)\), \(n = 3, 4, 5, \ldots\)

The shortest wavelength (series limit) corresponds to \(n = \infty\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{min}} = \dfrac{R_H}{4} \Rightarrow \lambda_{min} = \dfrac{4}{R_H} = \dfrac{4}{1{\cdot}097 \times 10^{7}} \approx 3{\cdot}646 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} \approx 364{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{nm}\).

answers.value: (iv) \(\approx 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J} \approx 1879\ \mathrm{MeV}\); (v) it needs extremely high temperatures; (vi) the electron is bound to the nucleus; (vii) e.g. it applies only to one-electron atoms
answers.working:
**(iv)** A proton and an antiproton have equal rest mass \(m_p\). The minimum photon energy is the rest mass energy of the pair (created at rest):

\(E_{min} = 2m_p c^2 = 2 \times 1{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-27} \times (3 \times 10^{8})^2 = 3{\cdot}006 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}\).

In eV: \(\dfrac{3{\cdot}006 \times 10^{-10}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1{\cdot}88 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{eV} \approx 1879\ \mathrm{MeV}\).

**(v)** In fusion, two positively charged light nuclei must come very close together, against their strong electrostatic repulsion. They get enough kinetic energy to do this only at extremely high temperatures (of the order of \(10^{7}\) K or more). Because the reaction is started and sustained by such high temperature, it is called a thermonuclear reaction.

**(vi)** The negative total energy shows that the electron is **bound** to the nucleus by the attractive force; it cannot escape on its own. Energy equal to the magnitude of the total energy (the ionisation energy) must be supplied from outside to free it.

**(vii)** One limitation: Bohr's theory applies only to hydrogen and hydrogen-like (single-electron) atoms; it cannot explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron. (Other acceptable answers: it cannot explain the fine structure of spectral lines, or the relative intensities of the lines.)

answers.value: (i) a microammeter; (ii) by doping with a pentavalent or trivalent impurity; (iii) the pd across the depletion layer that opposes diffusion; (iv) half-wave rectifier circuit
answers.working:
**(i)** In reverse bias the current is very small (of the order of microamperes), so Annie used a **microammeter** (\(\mu\mathrm{A}\)).

**(ii)** She **doped** the pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, such as silicon or germanium, by adding a very small amount of a suitable impurity: a **pentavalent** impurity (for example phosphorus, arsenic) gives an n-type semiconductor, and a **trivalent** impurity (for example boron, aluminium, indium) gives a p-type semiconductor.

**(iii)** When the p-n junction forms, electrons and holes diffuse across it and recombine, leaving immobile positive ions on the n-side and immobile negative ions on the p-side of the junction (the depletion region). These ions set up an electric field and a potential difference across the junction, directed so that it opposes further diffusion of majority carriers. This potential difference is the **potential barrier** (about \(0{\cdot}7\ \mathrm{V}\) for silicon and \(0{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{V}\) for germanium).

**(iv)** The labelled circuit diagram of a half wave rectifier shows: the ac input applied to the primary coil of a transformer; one end of the secondary coil connected to the p-side (anode) of a p-n junction diode D; the n-side (cathode) of the diode connected through a load resistance \(R_L\) back to the other end of the secondary coil. The dc output is taken across \(R_L\). (Waveforms, if drawn: a full sine wave at the input, and only the positive half cycles at the output, with gaps for the negative half cycles when the diode is reverse biased.)
